--- title: "The top science systems differ unusually widely in student AI use" subtitle: "Share of 15-year-olds who report using AI at least weekly to help them learn. Only 0.3% of 100,000 random groups of 11 systems were as spread out as these 11." description: "Among the 11 highest-scoring PISA 2025 science systems, the share of students using AI weekly ranges from 27% to 67%, more spread out than 99.7% of random groups of 11. A two-panel dot strip compares them with an illustrative random group drawn from the same 85 countries and economies. Built in R with ggplot2, ggtext and showtext." date: "2026-11-01" author: - name: "Steven Ponce" url: "https://stevenponce.netlify.app" citation: url: "https://stevenponce.netlify.app/data_visualizations/MakeoverMonday/2026/mm_2026_44.html" categories: ["MakeoverMonday", "2026"] tags: [ "makeover-monday", "pisa", "oecd", "education", "artificial-intelligence", "ai-in-education", "beeswarm", "dot-strip", "random-baseline", "variation", "ggplot2", "ggtext", "showtext", "2026" ] image: "thumbnails/mm_2026_44.png" format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 5 code-link: true code-fold: true code-tools: true code-summary: "Show code" editor_options: chunk_output_type: inline execute: freeze: true cache: true error: false message: false warning: false eval: true --- ### Original The original visualization comes from [PISA 2025 Results (Volume I)](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2025-results-volume-i_73451bc5-en.html). ![Original visualization](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poncest/MakeoverMonday/refs/heads/master/2026/Week_44/original_chart.png) ### Makeover ![Two-panel dot strip chart titled "The top science systems differ unusually widely in student AI use." Each dot is one of 85 countries and economies, placed by the share of 15-year-olds who report using AI at least weekly to help them learn; the same dots sit in the same positions in both panels, with the middle half of systems (about 44% to 53%) shaded. In the lower panel, the 11 highest-scoring systems in PISA 2025 science are highlighted and labeled. They range from 27% in Japan to 67% in Macao (China), and only Korea, Australia and New Zealand fall inside the middle half. Australia and New Zealand tie for 10th. The upper panel highlights one illustrative random group of 11, with most of its shares between 40% and 57%. Only 0.3% of 100,000 random groups of 11 were as spread out as the top 11. Source: OECD, PISA 2025 Results (Volume I), Table I.6.](mm_2026_44.png){#fig-1} ### [**Steps to Create this Graphic**]{.mark} #### [1. Load Packages & Setup]{.smallcaps} ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| label: load #| warning: false #| message: false #| results: "hide" ## 1. LOAD PACKAGES & SETUP ---- suppressPackageStartupMessages({ if (!require("pacman")) install.packages("pacman") pacman::p_load( tidyverse, ggtext, showtext, scales, glue, janitor, ggview, readxl, ggrepel, magick ) }) # Source utility functions suppressMessages( source(here::here("R/utils/fonts.R"))) source(here::here("R/utils/social_icons.R")) source(here::here("R/themes/base_theme.R")) ### |- figure size ---- fig_w <- 10 fig_h <- 5.05 fig_dpi <- 320 ### |- fonts ---- setup_fonts() fonts <- get_font_families() title_family <- fonts$title_1 text_family <- fonts$text cap_family <- fonts$caption ``` ```` ::: #### [2. Read in the Data]{.smallcaps} ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| label: read #| include: true #| eval: true #| warning: false xl_path <- here::here("data/MakeoverMonday/2026/PISA2025.xlsx") read_sheet <- function(sheet_name) { read_excel(xl_path, sheet = sheet_name, col_types = "text", na = character() ) |> clean_names() } df_raw <- read_sheet("PISA2025-Data") ``` ```` ::: #### [3. Examine the Data]{.smallcaps} ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| label: examine #| include: true #| eval: true #| results: 'hide' #| warning: false glimpse(df_raw) ``` ```` ::: #### [4. Tidy Data]{.smallcaps} ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| label: tidy #| warning: false ### |- one row per system with weekly-AI data ---- df <- df_raw |> transmute( country, sci = as.numeric(science_mean_score), ai_pct = 100 * as.numeric(students_using_ai_at_least_weekly_to_help_them_learn) ) |> filter(!is.na(ai_pct)) |> mutate(id = row_number()) n_sys <- nrow(df) ### |- top group: tie-preserving cut at the 10th science score ---- # Australia and New Zealand tie at 509 for 10th place; a top-10 cut would drop # one of them on an arbitrary tie-break, so the group keeps every system >= 509 k_target <- 10 cut_sci <- sort(df$sci, decreasing = TRUE)[k_target] top_set <- df |> filter(sci >= cut_sci) n_top <- nrow(top_set) ### |- random-group comparison (the test behind the subtitle) ---- # Spread = standard deviation of a group's shares. 100,000 random groups of # n_top systems are drawn from the 85; the share at least as spread out as the # top group is the reported rate. n_draws <- 100000 set.seed(2044) draws <- replicate(n_draws, sample.int(n_sys, n_top)) # n_top x n_draws draw_sd <- apply(matrix(df$ai_pct[draws], nrow = n_top), 2, sd) top_sd <- sd(top_set$ai_pct) median_sd <- median(draw_sd) share_ge <- mean(draw_sd >= top_sd) # illustrative group: the draw whose spread is closest to the median (first on # ties) -- fixed by rule, never chosen by how it looks pick <- which.min(abs(draw_sd - median_sd)) rand_ids <- draws[, pick] share_lab <- paste0(format(round(100 * share_ge, 1), nsmall = 1), "%") ### |- middle half of all 85 systems (the reference band) ---- q_lo <- unname(quantile(df$ai_pct, 0.25)) q_hi <- unname(quantile(df$ai_pct, 0.75)) n_top_in_band <- sum(top_set$ai_pct >= q_lo & top_set$ai_pct <= q_hi) ### |- beeswarm, computed once in physical points ---- x_lim <- c(20, 75) panel_w_in <- fig_w - 2 * 20 / 72 pt_per_pct <- panel_w_in * 72 / diff(x_lim) dot_size <- 2.1 d_pt <- dot_size * .pt * 0.75 + 1.2 swarm_y <- function(x_pt, d) { ord <- order(x_pt) y <- numeric(length(x_pt)) placed <- integer(0) offsets <- c(0, as.vector(rbind(seq_len(80), -seq_len(80))) * d * 0.5) for (i in ord) { for (cand in offsets) { if (length(placed) == 0 || all((x_pt[i] - x_pt[placed])^2 + (cand - y[placed])^2 >= d^2)) { y[i] <- cand break } } placed <- c(placed, i) } y } df <- df |> mutate(y = swarm_y(ai_pct * pt_per_pct, d_pt)) y_max <- max(abs(df$y)) row_gap <- 10 # Each panel gets only the height it needs (same pt-per-unit scale in both): # upper = heading + band label + swarm; lower = heading + two label rows + swarm head_clear <- 16 # heading block height + gap above the next element (pt) band_clear <- 28 # two-line band label + gap above the swarm (pt) label_h <- 10 # one label line (pt) axis_clear <- 10 # gap between the bottom label row and the axis (pt) panel_lims <- tibble( panel = c("random", "top"), y_lo = c(-(y_max + 8), -(y_max + row_gap + label_h + axis_clear)), y_hi = c( y_max + 6 + band_clear + head_clear, y_max + row_gap + label_h + head_clear + 4 ) ) y_range_total <- sum(panel_lims$y_hi - panel_lims$y_lo) panel_levels <- c("random", "top") plot_df <- bind_rows( df |> mutate(panel = "random", hi = id %in% rand_ids), df |> mutate(panel = "top", hi = id %in% top_set$id) ) |> mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = panel_levels)) ### |- labels for the top group---- label_size <- 2.6 char_pct <- label_size * .pt * 0.60 / pt_per_pct nudge_row <- function(x, w, gap = 0.8) { for (iter in 1:200) { moved <- FALSE for (i in seq_along(x)[-1]) { need <- (w[i - 1] + w[i]) / 2 + gap if (x[i] - x[i - 1] < need) { push <- (need - (x[i] - x[i - 1])) / 2 x[i - 1] <- x[i - 1] - push x[i] <- x[i] + push moved <- TRUE } } if (!moved) break } x } labels_df <- df |> filter(id %in% top_set$id) |> arrange(ai_pct) |> mutate( label = glue("{country} {round(ai_pct)}%"), side = if_else(row_number() %% 2 == 1, 1, -1), panel = factor("top", levels = panel_levels) ) |> group_by(side) |> mutate(label_x = nudge_row(ai_pct, nchar(label) * char_pct)) |> ungroup() |> mutate( label_y = side * (y_max + row_gap), vjust = if_else(side > 0, 0, 1) ) leaders <- labels_df |> mutate(label_id = row_number()) |> reframe( x = c(ai_pct, ai_pct, label_x), y = c(y + side * 4, label_y - side * 5, label_y - side * 2), .by = c(label_id, panel) ) ``` ```` ::: #### [5. Visualization Parameters]{.smallcaps} ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| label: params #| include: true #| warning: false ### |- plot aesthetics ---- colors <- get_theme_colors( palette = list( paper = "#f4f1ea", ink = "#2b2b2b", muted = "#6f6a63", accent = "#722F37", dot = "#c9c4ba", band = "#e6e0d4" ) ) clrs <- colors$palette col_paper <- clrs$paper col_ink <- clrs$ink col_muted <- clrs$muted col_accent <- clrs$accent col_dot <- clrs$dot col_band <- clrs$band ### |- titles and caption ---- title_text <- "The top science systems differ unusually widely in student AI use" subtitle_text <- paste0( "Share of 15-year-olds who report using AI at least weekly to help them learn.\n", glue("Only {share_lab} of {comma(n_draws)} random groups of {n_top} systems were as spread out as these {n_top}.") ) headings <- tibble( panel = factor(panel_levels, levels = panel_levels), label = c( glue("For comparison: a typical random group of {n_top}"), glue("The {n_top} highest-scoring systems in science") ), colour = c(col_muted, col_ink), x = x_lim[1], y = panel_lims$y_hi - 2 ) # right-aligned notes, one per panel: how each highlighted group was chosen panel_notes <- tibble( panel = factor(panel_levels, levels = panel_levels), x = x_lim[2], y = panel_lims$y_hi - 2, label = c( "Illustrative draw closest to median spread", "Australia and New Zealand tie for 10th" ) ) band_lab <- tibble( panel = factor("random", levels = panel_levels), x = (q_lo + q_hi) / 2, y = panel_lims$y_hi[1] - 2, label = glue("Middle half of\nall {n_sys} systems") ) note_text <- paste( glue("{n_sys} countries and economies with AI-use data; six without are not shown."), glue("Spread = standard deviation, compared with {comma(n_draws)} random groups of {n_top}."), "Country-level student reports; says nothing about AI's effect on scores." ) caption_text <- paste0( note_text, "
", create_mm_caption( mm_year = 2026, mm_week = 44, source_text = "OECD, PISA 2025 Results (Volume I), Table I.6" ) ) ### |- plot theme ---- base_theme <- create_base_theme(colors) weekly_theme <- extend_weekly_theme( base_theme, theme( plot.background = element_rect(fill = col_paper, colour = NA), panel.background = element_rect(fill = col_paper, colour = NA), panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(family = text_family, size = rel(0.7), colour = col_muted), axis.title = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), axis.line.x = element_line(colour = col_dot, linewidth = 0.4), strip.text = element_blank(), panel.spacing = unit(16, "pt"), legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text( family = title_family, size = rel(1.72), colour = col_ink, margin = margin(b = 6) ), plot.subtitle = element_text( family = text_family, size = rel(0.80), colour = col_muted, lineheight = 1.3, margin = margin(b = 10) ), plot.caption = element_textbox_simple( family = cap_family, size = rel(0.45), colour = col_muted, lineheight = 1.3, margin = margin(t = 10) ), plot.margin = margin(16, 20, 12, 20) ) ) theme_set(weekly_theme) ``` ```` ::: #### [6. Plot]{.smallcaps} ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| label: plot #| warning: false ### |- main plot ---- p <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = ai_pct, y = y)) + annotate( "rect", xmin = q_lo, xmax = q_hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = col_band ) + geom_path( data = leaders, aes(x = x, y = y, group = label_id), colour = col_accent, linewidth = 0.3 ) + geom_point( data = filter(plot_df, !hi), shape = 21, size = dot_size, fill = col_dot, colour = col_muted, stroke = 0.3 ) + geom_point( data = filter(plot_df, hi), shape = 21, size = dot_size + 0.3, fill = col_accent, colour = col_paper, stroke = 0.4 ) + geom_text( data = labels_df, aes(x = label_x, y = label_y, label = label, vjust = vjust), family = text_family, size = label_size, colour = col_accent ) + geom_text( data = headings, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label, colour = colour), hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", family = text_family, size = 3.4 ) + geom_text( data = panel_notes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), hjust = 1, vjust = 1, family = text_family, size = 2.6, colour = col_muted ) + geom_text( data = band_lab, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), vjust = 1, lineheight = 0.95, family = text_family, size = 3.1, colour = col_muted ) + scale_colour_identity() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(20, 70, 10), labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) + geom_blank( data = panel_lims |> mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = panel_levels)) |> pivot_longer(c(y_lo, y_hi), values_to = "y") |> mutate(ai_pct = mean(x_lim)), aes(x = ai_pct, y = y) ) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(0)) + facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") + coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lim, expand = FALSE, clip = "off") + labs(title = title_text, subtitle = subtitle_text, caption = caption_text) ``` ```` ::: #### [7. Save]{.smallcaps} ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| label: save #| warning: false ### |- save ---- main_path <- here::here("data_visualizations", "MakeoverMonday", "2026", "mm_2026_44.png") thumb_path <- here::here("data_visualizations", "MakeoverMonday", "2026", "thumbnails", "mm_2026_44.png") # Full-size version, for the QMD figure save_ggplot( plot = p, file = main_path, width = fig_w, height = fig_h, units = "in", dpi = 320, ) # Reduced-size thumbnail fs::dir_create(dirname(thumb_path)) magick::image_read(main_path) |> magick::image_resize("400") |> magick::image_write(thumb_path) ``` ```` ::: #### [8. References]{.smallcaps} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ##### Expand for References **Primary Data (Makeover Monday):** 1. Makeover Monday 2026 Week 44: [PISA 2025: Digital learning, AI and student performance](https://makeovermonday.vercel.app/dataset/pisa-2025) - Workbook: 91 countries and economies, 19 fields, extracted from Tables I.1 and I.6 of the report; 85 have weekly-AI-use data (Cambodia, Dushanbe, Kurdistan Region, Mauritius, Rwanda and Zambia do not). - Region and OECD-member columns were added by the dataset author; the About sheet cites an OECD-average sheet that is not in the file. - Change since 2022 carries no significance flags; Uzbekistan's +83 in science is flagged by the source as needing care. **Source Data:** 2. OECD (2026). *PISA 2025 Results (Volume I): Future-Ready Students*. OECD Publishing, Paris. [https://doi.org/10.1787/73451bc5-en](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2025-results-volume-i_73451bc5-en.html). Table I.6 (snapshot of digitalisation and AI); Table I.1 (performance). CC BY 4.0. **Original Visualization:** 3. OECD (2026), *PISA 2025 Results (Volume I)*: science proficiency levels for OECD countries, a seven-band diverging bar chart centred on Level 2. [OECD publication page](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2025-results-volume-i_73451bc5-en.html). **Related Analysis:** 4. OECD (2026). [Executive Summary, PISA 2025 Results (Volume I)](https://read.oecd-ilibrary.org/en/publications/pisa-2025-results-volume-i_73451bc5-en/full-report/executive-summary_3701b0ef.html). The source reports AI findings at the student level: students who use AI for specific schoolwork score lower, and weekly general users score about the same as non-users. This makeover works at the country level and makes no claim about effects. **Analysis Frame:** - **Measure:** share of 15-year-olds who report using AI at least weekly to help them learn (student questionnaire, country-level). - **Top group:** the 11 systems scoring 509 or higher in science. Australia and New Zealand tie at 509 for 10th, so both are included rather than broken by an arbitrary tie-break. - **Comparison:** standard deviation of the top group's shares (13.0 points) against 100,000 random groups of 11 drawn from the 85 (median 7.7). 0.28% were as spread out (seed 2044). - **Upper panel:** the random draw whose spread is closest to that median. It illustrates a typical group; it is not the test. - **Reference band:** middle half of all 85 systems, 43.8% to 52.5%; 3 of the 11 fall inside it. ::: #### [11. Custom Functions Documentation]{.smallcaps} ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ##### 📦 Custom Helper Functions This analysis uses custom functions from my personal module library for efficiency and consistency across projects. **Functions Used:** - **`fonts.R`**: `setup_fonts()`, `get_font_families()` - Font management with showtext - **`social_icons.R`**: `create_social_caption()` - Generates formatted social media captions - **`image_utils.R`**: `save_plot()` - Consistent plot saving with naming conventions - **`base_theme.R`**: `create_base_theme()`, `extend_weekly_theme()`, `get_theme_colors()` - Custom ggplot2 themes **Why custom functions?**\ These utilities standardize theming, fonts, and output across all my data visualizations. The core analysis (data tidying and visualization logic) uses only standard tidyverse packages. **Source Code:**\ View all custom functions → [GitHub: R/utils](https://github.com/poncest/personal-website/tree/master/R) :::
